_comment: The claims the smoke scenarios prove (#1055). A claim is a short promise with one number, stable forever. Its title is at most
twelve words (#1817); its page under live/smoke/claims/ gives its proofs. Proof is per provider (#1112): each providers.<name> cell
carries a status, an optional note and a list of proofs. A proof is a scenario that runs on that provider (scenario, command, minutes,
needs_go, needs_emulator, real_service, break_mode, evidence, an optional note), some steps of another claim's scenario on the same
provider (proven_by, that scenario's command, a note naming the steps), a gauntlet stage (stage "<estate>:<stage id>", resolved

against live/gauntlet.json, and a note saying what it asserts), or a Go test (#2288: go_test, go_package, gate, command, a note; see below). A scenario's header states its cell: "# CLAIM N (provider) - <title>. ~M min.".
demos lists the scenarios that prove no claim; they carry no CLAIM header and belong to no cell.

status is proven (every proof names a dated run: an evidence file with a date, a last_run, steps of such a scenario, a gauntlet stage that reads pass, or a recorded Go test run; a Go test proof with no recorded run yet is waiting, and stands beside the cell's dated proofs without counting as one) or n/a (the substrate has no such concept).

go_test names a test in go_package ("./pkg/x"; a subtest is Test/Sub). With no gate it runs in CI's fast tier, its command is the go test that runs exactly it, and its dated run is a CI run at a recorded commit; with a gate (the environment variable it skips without) its command is the just recipe that sets that variable, and its dated run is a maintainer run with its log. `go run ./tools/gotest-record` writes both under live/smoke/evidence/go-test/, and nothing else does.

kind "product-scenario" (#2299) cites one recorded row of a CI product's scenario run: repo (INTENTIUS/<product>), scenario (the product's scenario id), claim (the product's claim id), commit (full sha), date (YYYY-MM-DD), engine_version (the choudoufu release the row ran, X.Y.Z) and a note, the same kind and keys plunge and sql-yodeler use. Its row is kept under live/smoke/evidence/product-scenario/, and it counts only when engine_version is the newest release in live/history. It stands beside the cell's engine proofs and never replaces one (ruling E on chant#4586). The other kinds carry no kind field.
A promise with no proof is a GitHub issue, never a claim.

last_run on a scenario proof is the last result measured for it, carried until a newer run replaces it: status, claim, commit, date (YYYY-MM-DD) and version. live/claims_last_run_test.go holds each entry to this file's history at 958bcf7f2d.
substrate lists the providers the promise applies to: every cell that is not n/a.
retired lists numbers that are no longer claims of their own; a number is never reused. One with claim and provider lives in that claim's cell;
demo: true is a scenario that is now a demo; covered_by names the proof that shows the same thing (a scenario, a stage or a Go test); merged_into is a whole claim nested in the named one;
reserved: true is a number held back with no claim behind it.
real_service: true marks a proof that runs against the provider's real account, maintainer-run (SMOKE_REAL_AWS=1 for aws).
needs_emulator: true marks a Kubernetes proof that also brings up the pinned floci emulator for an S3-backed record store.
Scenario file names may carry a k8s- prefix for readability. The provider a scenario proves is the providers.<name> key that names its cell, never its file name (#1598, #1593).

proofs.note: A scheduled delete (Secrets Manager's DeleteSecret with a recovery window, like KMS's ScheduleKeyDeletion) answers success and leaves the resource in the account, tags included. The plan after it is empty, as stock's is, with no second destroy and no refusal of the swept, still-marked object (#1599).

BREAK=1 removes the finalizer before the destroying apply and requires the opposite outcome - the object gone in one apply and the replan empty - because without that control the scenario would read identically if choudoufu simply never deleted a ConfigMap

BREAK=1 runs the identical namespace delete and then asserts what a sweep that never saw it would plan, "No changes.", over the real plan; that assertion must fail, and the control passes only when the plan instead proposes the three creates, because without it the creates of step 4 would read the same if the plan proposed them whatever the cluster held
proofs.note: A namespace deleted under a converged estate takes its objects with it, and the plan reads them as gone, the same plan stock makes on the same cluster. Step 7, a deleted record-store namespace, is claim 29's (#1765).

kubernetes.note: The sweep is one cluster-wide, label-selected list per kind, and controller-made objects are excluded before anything reaches a delete. An object no natural key declares is bound by the block its address annotation names (#1640), an orphan otherwise; two objects whose annotations claim one block are refused as a collision (#1641).

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 manufactures the corruption the claim guards against and passes only by catching it

proofs.note: Two writers on one record, at the store: once one writer's conditional PUT has moved the record, the other's PUT carrying the version it read is refused with a version conflict, against an in-process S3 that enforces If-Match and If-None-Match as S3 does. A PutObject with no If-Match, the corruption the two-writers-one-record scenario's BREAK arm built until #2288, fails it. plunge's TestPlungeS3StoreConformance runs the same suite on floci.
The loser of the race at the write-back: a record that moved after this run's plan read it is not overwritten, and the run stops on an error naming both versions.

Real AWS, maintainer-run with SMOKE_REAL_AWS=1, and only when pkg/staterecord/s3.go changes (#2288 ruling Q3): the conditional-write suite on four real buckets, SSE-S3, SSE-KMS under the AWS-managed key and under a customer managed key, and DSSE-KMS. Under the three KMS flavours the ETag is not the payload's MD5, and the store must treat it as opaque. Its last run, as step 2 of the retired scenario cas-holds-under-every-sse-flavour, is live/smoke/evidence/cas-holds-under-every-sse-flavour.lastrun.json (2026-09-19).

Step 3 of claim 29's Kubernetes scenario (#1392): an apply killed with SIGKILL, the very next run carries on, and nothing lock-shaped is left in the records namespace. Step 3's BREAK control plants a Lease and a lock-named Secret and requires its check to fail.

Two writers parked on the wire over one resourceVersion and released one at a time on a real API server (#1441): twelve rounds, update against update and create against create, each landing exactly one write and refusing the other with a VersionConflictError naming both versions, with no trace of the loser's payload. CHOUDOUFU_K8S_RECORD_RACE_BREAK=1 swaps each write for the stock backend's read-then-update, and the test must then fail with both writes landed. Step 10 of k8s-records-in-the-cluster until #2288.

claims.title: A crash is fixed by re-running

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 strips the ownership markers off everything the killed apply created, leaving the same objects in the same account with no ownership on them; the re-run must then be unable to bind and must build a duplicate VPC, which is stock's behaviour, and a strip that left a marker behind fails the control rather than passing it. BREAK_EARLY_RECORD=1 rebuilds choudoufu with the mid-apply record write switched off (go build -overlay, needs Go, refuses a release binary), so no record is written until the walk is over; the killed run must then leave no record for the inline policy, the password or the effect, the next plan must propose generating the password again, and the re-run must leave two inline policies on the group (#1944)
proofs.note: A record-backed or record-carried instance's record is written the moment its apply step returns (#1944): the killed run leaves records for an aws_iam_group_policy whose name the provider assigned, a random_password and a terraform_data with a provisioner, and the re-run keeps one inline policy, the same password and an effect that ran once. Step 7 deletes the cache, the lock file and the whole .terraform directory, and the next plan from a fresh init is empty.

kubernetes.note: An apply SIGKILLed between one ConfigMap's create and the next leaves one labelled object; the next plan binds it by its label, namespace and name, proposes only what was never reached, and the re-run keeps its uid and replans empty.

proofs.note: The gauntlet's day2_crash stage on a kind estate: an apply creating two ConfigMaps is interrupted by a real SIGTERM the instant the first create commits; the next plan proposes exactly the remainder and binds the created object by its tofu-estate label, namespace and name, matching stock's own plan; one recovery apply finishes and the replan is empty. Its BREAK asserts nothing is proposed and must fail.

claims.title: The record store refuses what it can't trust

proofs.note: Versioning, a lifecycle rule expiring noncurrent versions, and the public-access block are each asserted, and a bucket missing one, or a setting that cannot be read, is a finding naming it. CheckBucketContract reporting no findings, the a-wrong-bucket-is-refused scenario's BREAK arm until #2288, fails it.
A bucket that fails its contract is refused on the estate's first contact, by name, and again on every first contact until it is fixed; nothing is written to it.
Every apply asserts the contract before it writes: a failing setting refuses the apply naming the setting and the bucket, and a setting that could not be read is refused like one that failed.
allow_insecure waives the settings it names and no others: the assertions it does not name still refuse.
First contact under a waiver goes ahead past the waived setting alone.

A waiver names what it waives on every run: a first apply, a plan once the state cache exists, and a second apply each print the warning once. The a-waiver-names-what-it-waives scenario's BREAK patch, the warning emitted only while the state cache is absent, fails it on run two (#2288).
The bulk read is a LIST and a fan-out of GETs, and one failed GET fails the whole read: it never returns a map short of a key the listing named (#1355).

The fan-out under the bulk read reports success only for work it did. The pre-#1355 fan-out that swallowed a failed GET, the a-bulk-read-is-complete-or-it-fails scenario's BREAK arm until #2288, fails it.
A declared record the store's listing names and its read answers as absent is refused at the plan, naming the key, rather than planned as not created yet.

The same contradiction on the path a destroy takes, through the run cache: the build an `apply -destroy` plans from fails, naming the key, where it would otherwise leave the instance out and report one of two destroyed as a success (#1355). It pins the one refuseListedButReadAsAbsent call, which the scenario's BREAK_CROSSCHECK arm removed until #2288.

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 takes the three fences away and requires what they refused to go through: the plan role is given cluster-wide secret reads and must then read the other estate's records, the admission policy is removed and the cross-estate write into a record Secret must then land, and the scoped identity whose first contact the cluster contract passed is given cluster-wide secret reads, after which the same first contact must be refused on read_isolation. Step 11 rebuilds choudoufu with go build -overlay: a binary whose waiver warning is emitted on an estate's first run only must have its second run refused by step 11's check for naming no waiver. Steps 2, 3, 8 and 9 each have a control that runs the step's own check function against a world built to fail it and requires the failure by name: the record Secrets stripped of their annotation and then their label, a planted Lease and a lock-named Secret, the Role short one verb given that verb so the same apply goes through and leaves records behind, and a write between the two resourceVersion dumps and a dump of a namespace holding no record; the listings behind steps 3, 8 and 9 are also run through a kubeconfig that reaches no server and must fail rather than read as empty
proofs.note: Steps 6, 8 and 11 are this claim: the store checks the records namespace, its RBAC scope, encryption at rest and the estate boundary once, on an estate's first contact, before it writes a record; a Role one verb short is refused at first contact, naming the verb, with nothing left behind; a waiver names what it waives on every run and `choudoufu live-cluster` ignores it. Steps 2 to 5 and 9 are claim 28's, and step 3 claim 2's. Steps 1, 7, 10 and 12 are Go tests since #2288; the evidence file is the run of 2026-09-21, which still carried them.
Step 7 of claim 1's Kubernetes scenario (#1765): the record store's namespace deleted under a converged estate is refused by name on the plan and on the apply, and nothing is written.

The shared Store contract on a real API server: the conditional create, update and delete, the absent-key answers and the listing rules, the cases LocalStore and S3Store are held to. client-go's fake clientset assigns no resourceVersion, so this is the run that means anything. Step 1 of k8s-records-in-the-cluster until #2288.
The namespace_access assertion refuses an identity short of the store's verbs, naming the verbs it lacks. With the four below, step 7 of k8s-records-in-the-cluster until #2288.
read_isolation refuses an identity that can read another estate's records namespace, naming that namespace.
encryption_at_rest refuses a cluster whose Secrets are not encrypted at rest, and one that cannot say is reported as not checked, never as a pass.
estate_boundary refuses each way the boundary policy can be installed without being in force, an unbound policy among them.
An absent records namespace is refused in the same words, and with the same kubectl line, as the store's own NamespaceMissingError.
The store's listing reads every page of a paged LIST on a real API server. With the test below, step 12 of k8s-records-in-the-cluster until #2288.
A listing whose second page is answered 410 Expired fails whole, List and GetAll alike, and never returns the first page as the estate.

claims.title: No secret survives unless you let it

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 applies the same estate under secrets = "store" and runs the identical scan over the identical set of files, which must then find the password (it finds it in the record and the cache); a scan that finds nothing there fails the run, because its zero under refuse would prove nothing
proofs.note: Under refuse the argument is proposed on every plan, rotated or not, and the scenario asserts both arms (#1503).

kubernetes.note: Under strict { secrets = "refuse" } on a kind cluster, a random_password is refused by name with nothing written, a kubernetes_secret_v1 fed from the environment applies with no state cache and the value in no kept file, and the replan is empty because the API server returns the data; a rotated value is proposed (#1873).

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 applies the identical estate under secrets = "store" and runs the identical scan, which must find the value (it finds it in the state cache); a scan that finds nothing there fails the run, because its zero under refuse would prove nothing

BREAK=1 removes the estate's own ignore_tags declaration - the one piece of configuration the claim is about, not a choudoufu code path - and runs the identical out-of-band AWS CLI tag write; it passes only when the plan now proposes an update naming the tag, because choudoufu has no tag-diffing of its own to defeat with a build overlay: a resource's tags are planned entirely by the real hashicorp/aws provider process, the same one a stock run talks to
proofs.note: A tag another account's automation or an AWS service adds out of band churns nothing once the estate tells its provider to ignore that key, and an edit to a tag the estate declares plans (#1624).

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 runs the identical kubectl command against a key the configuration does NOT declare - same object, same --overwrite, one key different - and requires the opposite outcome, "No changes.", with the label still on the object afterwards. Without it every plan the main arm requires would read the same if choudoufu simply planned on any difference between the configuration and the live object, and step 5's point - that the provider's computed_fields rule still keeps the server's own keys out of the plan - would be scenery. It then runs one control for steps 8 and 9 together: the same two working directories on record_store "local", where the second one has no record to read and must plan "No changes." instead of the removal, which is what a Kubernetes estate on the implied store gives its second operator today.
proofs.note: A key the configuration never declared (the API server's kubernetes.io/metadata.name, a controller's annotation) stays the server's and churns nothing, because kubernetes_manifest's computed_fields reads the prior manifest. A label or annotation edited, added or deleted in the configuration plans the one in-place update stock plans, and a second working directory with no record of its own removes the same label when the estate shares its records.
